caption:
6 things I wish I knew when I started my coaching business 👇

⚡ Clear marketing > clever marketing – Trying to sound smart and “unique” will actually lose you sales. Your ideal clients don’t need to be impressed—they need to understand exactly how you help them in the simplest way possible.

⚡ Clients come from conversations, not from a website – I wasted time thinking I needed the perfect website when, in reality, every sale I made came from a real conversation. Don’t waste time or money building a website if you don’t have clients yet.

⚡ You don’t need more strategies—you need to refine one and double down – Instead of constantly chasing new ways to get clients, pick ONE strategy, make it as efficient as possible, and scale it. More strategies = more distractions.

⚡ Stop wasting time on Canva – Yes, branding matters, but changing your colors or tweaking your graphics for hours does nothing for sales. Once you have a clean, simple brand, leave it alone and focus on what actually moves the needle.

⚡ Systems = freedom – If you don’t follow a system, your business will run you. Make a list of what needs to be done, schedule it, and do the highest-priority task first. Otherwise, you’ll always feel like you “should” be doing something and never feel like you have actual time off.

⚡ Mentors fast-track results – I remember wondering if business coaches were just trying to sell me a program, but when I was serious about growing, so I took the leap and hired with @rossjohnsxn — the investment was a lot more than I felt comfortable with but I definitely got what I paid for 🤣🤣🤣

caption:
Top 5 digital marketing trends for 2024

Trend #1: Companies will create podcasts over blogs

Ideally, you should have both, but podcasting it a blue ocean.

There are 1 billion blogs. And there are 7.8 billion people in the world.

That’s 1 blog for every 7.8 people.

On the flip side, there are 4.2 million podcasts.

That’s 1 podcast for every 1857 people.

Trend #2: Companies will spend time on the less popular social networks.

Although Facebook, YouTube, and Instagram are the more popular social networks, they don’t provide the best return on ad spend.

Trend #3: Marketing moats will become non-existent, other than brands.

What makes Jordan shoes special isn’t the quality of the shoes. There are a lot of other high-quality shoes.

It’s the brand (Jump Man logo).

What made Kylie Cosmetics popular was the brand… not the quality of the product.

Technology has made it easier to copy the competition.

But the one thing that can separate you is your brand.

Trend #4: You’ll change the way you write content

There are two things in this trend.

First off, it used to be where 2300-word articles were the ones ranking at the top of Google.

Then it became 1447-word articles.

It’s because of tiktokification. The average user spends 95 minutes a day consuming short-form content.

And the second thing is human-written content will outperform AI-written content.

94.12% of the time, human-written content outranked AI-generated content.

But what’s interesting is more marketers are relying on AI to create their content.

This should make it easier for your content to stand out.

Trend #5: Marketing will no longer focus on 1 region

Big companies are already doing this. Mid-size companies and startups will start.

Instead of just focusing on the US or the UK, you’ll have no choice but to expand globally.

It’s where the money is.

Plus it is less competitive in most regions outside of the US.

caption:
Want a marketing strategy that fits what you sell and how your clients buy? Comment “CEO” to learn more.

A business selling a $67 digital product and a business selling $15,000 private coaching probably shouldn’t have identical marketing strategies.

One needs enough volume for the math to work.

One may need launches, trainings, webinars, paid traffic and enough trust to turn that attention into a $2K decision.

The other can build a very profitable business through a much smaller number of high-trust relationships, referrals, repeat buyers and people who have been quietly paying attention for months (sometimes years).

Neither is better. They’re different buying environments.

This is why I’m always cautious when someone says:
“Post 3x a day.”
“Run this funnel.”
“Start a webinar.”
“Just build relationships.”
“Put everything evergreen.”

Okay... what are you selling? 😂

Because the marketing strategy that makes sense for someone selling a $67 product at volume may make absolutely no sense for someone who needs 10–20 private clients a year.

Price point + delivery model + buyer + traffic source should influence your marketing strategy.

Don’t copy the marketing strategy without understanding the business model behind it.

caption:
Step by step chat sales process 

“I can’t close sales on chat”

I hear this all the time from my coaching clients…

They think they need hour long sales calls to sell anything over $1K

Truth is: You can make millions without even picking up the phone

“But I don’t have any leads”

If you’re making content on IG and getting followers… every single person is a conversation waiting to happen

1. Start the Conversation

The key is to open the conversation the right way

If you mess this up… you’ll get put in the friend zone instantly. And nobody likes that;)

So here’s what to send:

Msg 1 - Hey [Name]
Msg 2 - Thanks for the follow:)
Msg 3 - Are you here for the content/vids or are you looking to [get in shape, grow your biz, get more sales, etc.]

If they lean in, move to the next step

2. Qualifying

I call this the Doctor Frame

When you’re a doctor, treatment without diagnosis is malpractice

Think of your conversations in the same light… Seek to understand rather than sell

Here are 3 questions to ask:

Tell me a bit about your situation? [team size, current weight, marketing spend, etc.]
Where do you want to go in the next [insert time frame]?
What are you struggling with to get there?

These questions seem basic, but the magic is in the follow up

Whatever pain comes up from those answers, double down on it

Just like a doctor, push on the bruise

If they’re qualified AND want help, that’s where closing comes in

3. Closing

The key to chat sales is to sell from the heels. Give them an opportunity to lean in.

Here are 3 questions that will get them swim towards you:

Do you want help so you can [outcome]?
Have you ever worked w/ a [coach, agency, etc.]?
I just launched this [product or service] with [insert high-level details] would you be interested?

If they show interest, this sets the stage for the offer. If they aren’t receptive, feel free to lean out.

Try makes it sound like you may fail. Say explore instead. Explore makes it sound like an opportunity to grow. Number three, don't say buy now. Say limited quantity instead. It increases the urgency to buy. Number four, don't say expensive. Expensive makes it sound overpriced. Say premium instead. Premium makes it sound more valuable. Number five, don't say cheap. When you’re a doctor, treatment without diagnosis is malpractice

Tell me a bit about your situation? [team size, current weight, marketing spend, etc.]
Where do you want to go in the next [insert time frame]?

caption:
What's the best way to close a client on a discovery call?

I'm not a big fan of closing someone on a discovery call.

A discovery call is probably thirty minutes to an hour. If you really want to build trust and rapport and truly understand the pain points of that business, that is what the discovery call is for. To discover if there is an actual fit.

A lot of people do a one call close. I prefer a two call close.

The discovery call is purely there to discover and see synergies. We use the full half an hour to an hour to truly understand the business. What is the business truly like? What are the bottlenecks? What are you struggling with? Where are you truly now, margin wise, profit wise, revenue wise?

Only if we feel we can add value do we schedule a demonstration call and show how we can help.

The other reason is attention span. People only have about thirty minutes. The moment the call goes over thirty to forty minutes they're losing focus, so when you start pitching your services they're not paying as much attention as you want them to.

That's why we like to start a new call fresh a few days later, after we've done our own due diligence and our own bit of research.

So that's why we do a two call close, mainly.

'Sell me this pen' is one of the many famous scenes from Martin Scorsese's The Wolf of Wall Street (2013). That scene becomes the inspiration for this new ad for Alfa Romeo Junior (agency: Migrante Agency), featuring 'Berlin' (Pedro Alonso) of Money Heist (La Casa de Papel) fame! 

The ad is titled 'The Salesman', in line with the scene from The Wolf of Wall Street where Leonardo DiCaprio, portraying Jordan Belfort, the 1990s penny stockbroker, asks a room full of salesmen at a seminar to sell him a pen. Here, Pedro Alonso asks the people in the room to sell him the car. Who manages to 'sell 'the car to Pedro (and how) is the crux of the ad.

Interestingly, Jordan Belfort later (after his incarceration) spoke about this scene (On YouTube: https://tinyurl.com/sellme-thispen). Apparently, there is a right way to respond when someone asks you to sell them something, as per Jordan! When someone says, 'Sell me this pen', the first thing to do is to NOT directly start selling the product, but to ask questions. Questions to understand the context, motivation, and needs of the person asking to sell the pen. 

In the Alfa Romeo Junior ad too, the 'winner' asks Pedro a question that makes him think about his context to the car, and based on the question, he seems convinced! The question in this ad is an emotionally loaded question that cleverly alludes to the car's nature/quality!

PS: The choice of the song in the ad is perfect - Donna Summer's 1977 chartbuster, 'I Feel Love'!

caption:
Your personal brand is not a group project.

Someone asked me:

“What happens when you want to include a business partner’s perspective in your personal brand?”

My answer?

It’s not *people* branding.

It’s *personal* branding.

One person.

Your entire life is already built around compromise.

What your clients want.

What your partner wants.

What your kids want.

Where to go.

What to eat.

What to say.

So ask yourself:

Do you really want to compromise on who you are, too?

Other people can contribute to the business.

They can disagree with you.

They can have their own point of view.

But they don’t get to define you.

Here’s the rule I try to live by:

If making you happy requires me to stop being me, I’m not interested.

Your personal brand should sound like you.

Think like you.

Believe like you.

Otherwise, whose brand are you building?

caption:
Should you build a personal brand? YES.

Should you post random content that speaks to everyone and no one at the same time? NO.

Building a personal page on instagram and building a personal brand (hence the word “brand”) are two different things.

A strong brand needs a clear core message. 

This message must connect your brand’s main value to what you sell. It helps people know why you exist and why they should care. 

Does that mean you shouldn’t post about your life? 🤔

Of course not.

-If you’re out eating at a restaurant with your girlfriends…turn that post into something that connects to your offer. 

-If you’re lounging by a pool on a Tuesday…turn that post into something that connects to your offer. 

-If you’re frustrated and want to vent about it to your followers…turn that post into something that connects to your offer. 

Thats why strategy is so freaking important.

The good news is, you can fix this immediately. 👇🏽

If you feel like you have random stuff on your page go through each post and ask yourself this question: 

“Does this post represent me, who I want to attract, and who would actually benefit from my offer?”

If the answer is no, it can go 💪🏽

Thoughts are welcome below 🤓👇🏽

caption:
When is the right age to start a business? 🤔

In this conversation, a young interviewer asks an experienced entrepreneur for advice about starting a company. The speaker explains that before giving advice, three important things must be understood about a person:

• Who they are
• What they have
• What they truly want

He also talks about what he calls the “Zuckerberg effect.” Because of stories like Mark Zuckerberg, many young people today believe they must achieve massive success at a very young age.

According to the speaker, this pressure can be misleading.

He suggests that the earlier someone starts a business, the lower their success rate may be, mainly because experience, networks, and understanding of the market are still developing.

In his view, the “sweet spot” to start a company is between 30 and 35 years old, when people usually have more knowledge, resources, and clarity about what they want.

The core message: entrepreneurship is not a race.
Success often comes from experience, patience, and realistic expectations.

caption:
Advice for young entrepreneurs is as simple as it gets — and ignoring it is why most startups die.

He doesn’t complicate it. Before you deliver any product or service, get paid. Not after. Not on credit. Not “we’ll settle next month.” Upfront.

Why this matters for startups:
→ Cash flow kills more businesses than bad ideas
→ Credit-based models drain small companies fast
→ Getting paid first means you’re never funding someone else’s business
→ Immediate revenue removes dependency on loans or investors

And his encouraging point? There are at least a thousand business opportunities in India that can run on this payment-first model. From services to digital products to subscriptions — the options are everywhere.

The businesses that survive aren’t always the most innovative. They’re the ones that get paid on time.

Stop chasing revenue on paper. Start collecting cash in hand.

Money in the bank beats invoices in the inbox. Every time.

caption:
Michael Seibel learned one of Silicon Valley’s most important startup lessons while building Justin.tv, the company that eventually evolved into Twitch and sold to Amazon for nearly $1 billion in 2014. The original product was far from perfect. In fact, like many successful startups, it looked incomplete and often broken in its earliest days.

Seibel has long argued that founders spend far too much time trying to build the perfect product before launching. The reality is that startups learn by putting something into the hands of real users, collecting feedback, and improving rapidly. Most of the insights that shape great companies only appear after launch, not before it. His advice is ship earlier than you’re comfortable with. 

The founders who move fastest are usually the ones willing to launch something imperfect, learn from customers, and iterate relentlessly. Waiting for perfection often delays the very feedback needed to build a product people actually want.

Instagram co-founder Kevin Systrom says one of the most important lessons in entrepreneurship is that founders don’t need to be the best at every skill, but they need to know enough to be dangerous. Early on, that means learning enough to take an idea out of your head, turn it into something real, and put it in front of the world before you have an entire team of specialists around you.

Systrom says the company eventually reached a point where many of Instagram’s roughly 170 employees were far better than him at the individual skills required to build and grow the product. His role as a founder was increasingly about creating an idea talented people wanted to be part of, then bringing in people capable of taking different pieces of that idea much further than he could alone.

For Systrom, being a capable founder is less about mastering every discipline and more about having enough range to get an idea moving. Once the company starts working, the next skill is attracting people who can raise the level of what you started and turn the original idea into something much bigger.

caption:
4 things nobody taught me before I started my business. And not knowing them is exactly why most entrepreneurs struggle.

1. Return on Investment. You spent 100 rupees, how much came back? Agar jawab nahi pata, that’s not a strategy. That’s just spending money and hoping for the best.

2. Cash flow. Profit on paper aur account mein actual paisa, dono alag hain. If money isn’t moving, the business isn’t breathing. Doesn’t matter how good your P&L looks.

3. Customer Acquisition Cost and Lifetime Value. What does it cost to get one customer, and how much will they pay you over time? If what you spend is more than what they give, tum baar baar toot rahe ho.

4. Break-even point. How many sales do you need just to cover every single expense? Yeh nahi pata toh you’re running blind, no matter how busy you feel.

Learn your numbers before your numbers teach you. Because that lesson is always expensive.

caption:
Know who you are before you decide to become an entrepreneur.

Entrepreneurs jump off a cliff and try to build the plane on the way down. 

You have to be able to do that.

In the mid 90s, I was running my own asset management company and we were getting our asses kicked. 

A Goldman colleague comes to visit, sees the operation, gets excited and says he wants to leave and do the same thing.

I said — can I show you something first?

I walked him down the hall and opened a closet. Inside was $850,000 worth of servers and switches.

I said — you see that? That’s my summer house in the Hamptons.

Are you willing to put your summer house in a closet in Midtown Manhattan?

If yes, leave Goldman and start your business. 

If no, shut up and enjoy your career there. There’s absolutely nothing wrong with that.

The big message is simple: Know who you are, know what you’re capable of, know what you actually like doing.

Entrepreneurship is incredible. It’s also brutal. 

Make sure you know which version you’re signing up for.

caption:
Everyone's sharing the same advice.

Same tips. Same frameworks. Same "3 steps to success."

That's why nobody's listening yet.

Here's what the best entrepreneurs do differently:

1. Go deeper than everyone else.
- Don't share surface level tips. Dig into the real problem behind the problem. When you go deep, you stop sounding like everyone else and start changing lives.

2. Your limits are your advantage.
- No budget. No big team. No fancy gear. Good. Constraints force creativity. The thing holding you back might be the thing that makes you stand out.

3. Stop asking "how." Start asking "who."
- If you're doing everything yourself, you're building a job. Not a business. Find the right people to handle everything else so you can focus on your message.

4. Be the twin, not the titan.
- Stop trying to compete with the biggest names. You win by being relatable. Be the person who's just a few steps ahead of your audience. That's who they'll trust.

5. Out-teach your competition.
- You don't have to be the best. You just have to care the most. Answer the questions your competitors are too busy to answer. That's how you win.

Lay one brick today.

I want to see you win.

➝ 𝗙𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄 @evancarmichael

caption:
When people tell the story of a successful startup, they usually talk about the founder.⁠
I've learned the companies that last have something else in common.⁠
Builders.⁠
⁠
They're the people who quietly turn vision into momentum.⁠
The ones who see what needs to be done and do it.⁠
The ones every founder hopes to find.⁠
⁠
Here are five things I've learned about them.⁠
1. They don't wait for permission.⁠
Builders don't spend their time asking whose job something is.⁠
If something helps the company move forward, they step in.⁠
Not because they have to.⁠
Because they care.⁠
⁠
2. They run toward the hard problems.⁠
Startups are messy.⁠
Priorities shift.⁠
Resources are limited.⁠
Builders don't waste energy pointing out what's broken.⁠
They help figure out what comes next.⁠
⁠
3. They create clarity when everything feels chaotic.⁠
When everyone else feels overwhelmed, builders simplify.⁠
They help people focus on what matters most.⁠
And that momentum becomes contagious.⁠
⁠
4. They make the people around them better.⁠
They share what they know.⁠
They coach without being asked.⁠
They celebrate other people's wins.⁠
The best builders don't just build companies.⁠
They build people.⁠
⁠
5. They leave everything stronger than they found it.⁠
A process.⁠
A product.⁠
A customer relationship.⁠
A teammate.⁠

Come 50 Cent ha fatto 100 milioni vendendo acqua.

caption:
Three startups, three different founders, yet remarkably similar lessons emerged from their experiences. Each founder believed they understood what customers wanted, but some important decisions were made without gathering enough direct feedback from the people they were trying to serve. This highlights one of the most important principles of building a successful business: assumptions are not a substitute for listening to customers. Another challenge was how the products were presented, with claims that sometimes made them appear more different or distinctive than customers ultimately experienced. Even small differences between expectations and reality can affect how people perceive a company. Once trust begins to weaken, rebuilding it can take significant time and consistent effort. The broader lesson for entrepreneurs is simple: talk to customers early, test ideas before investing heavily, communicate honestly, and make improvements based on real-world feedback. A great product is not only about having a creative idea; it is also about understanding what people actually need and delivering an experience that matches what you promise.

caption:
This is how you land your first freelancing client:

Honesty, Evidence, Incentive.

1. Honesty: Don’t try to fool anybody, they may not know they’re your first, but they know they’re early adopters. Play into it. Everyone likes an underdog. Now, you don’t want to give them impression that you’ll need a lot of hand holding and that working with you will be difficult, but do give the impression that you’re scrappy and you’re going to wear their jersey and advocate for their success.
2. Evidence: It’s already hard enough to get clients at the start of your career. If you don’t have a portfolio, it’s nearly impossible. Take a week or so and create a few examples of the end result of working with. Remember, a portfolio isn’t the same thing as a resume, it’s not a representation of who you’ve worked with, it’s a demonstration of the solution you’re offering.
3. Incentive: Let’s be real here, if you’re hiring someone who’s untested and unproven in the field, you’re taking a bit of a risk. So de-risk that decision for your potential clients by competing on price (this is one of the only times I offer this advice). Just make sure you don’t offer to do it for free, because that’s bad for the project, and make sure you establish that this is a one time thing for the chance to earn their business, so you can charge for your value on future projects with them.

caption:
3 productivity hacks that actually help you get things done👇

1. The 2-Minute Rule
If a task feels overwhelming, tell yourself you only have to do it for two minutes.
Open the document. Start the email. Write the first sentence.

Starting removes the mental resistance, and most of the time you’ll naturally keep going once you begin.

How to try it today:
Pick one task you’ve been avoiding and set a 2-minute timer. Just start.

2. Write things down (physically).
Your brain is great at thinking, not holding information.

When you write things down on paper, you:
• remember things better
• clear mental clutter
• stop constantly trying to “keep everything in your head”

How to try it today:
Take 3 minutes and write tomorrow’s to-do list on paper before bed.

3. Change your environment.
Your environment quietly controls your focus.

If your phone is next to you, your brain is waiting for it to light up.

How to try it today:
Put your phone in another room while you work on one task.
Even 20–30 minutes of distraction-free focus can change your entire day.

Tiny systems like this make productivity feel easy instead of exhausting. ✨

Here’s my Top 10 Productivity Tips for an Entrepreneur 💡 
Number 1: Reframe your goals into SMART goals
Let’s break down each component the SMART goal framework a bit more:
The S stands for Specific. You want to clearly define your goal with specific details.
The M stands for Measurable: You need to establish a concrete criteria to track and measure your progress. 
The A stands for Achievable: It’s important to set goals that are realistic and attainable. Consider your resources and capabilities to ensure that your goal is within reach. 
The R stands for Relevant: Make sure that your goal is relevant and meaningful so that it directly contributes to your future vision.
The T stands for Time-bound: You’ll want to set a specific timeframe or deadline for achieving your goal.

caption:
👩🏼‍💻If you want a corporate job you need to be taken seriously and you need to know how to act. 

It’s ok if you were never taught, let me teach you interview etiquette. 

When you are being interviewed you are being hosted so act accordingly. 

🔹Say please and thank you, sit up straight, and participate in the conversation. 

🤝You need to know how to shake hands. 

If you are uncomfortable shaking hands, practice. 

First impressions matter and if you give me a limp handshake I will wonder why. 

❌Do NOT ask for coffee with cream & sugar, I am NOT a barista. Just ask for water or accept whatever I offer- do not make a crazy request. 

❌When you walk into the interview room, do NOT wait for me to tell you where to sit. 

✅Just sit opposite of me. 

✅When you sit down, always put your hands on the table. If you put your hands in your lap you look nervous and untrustworthy. 

✅Throughout the job interview you should be taking notes on a pad of paper in your padfolio NOT on your phone. 

When I ask you if you have questions, you need to have great questions prepared about next steps in the interview process. 

❌Do NOT ask me “Are there any reasons why you wouldn’t want to hire me?” because no one is going to be honest with you 

✅Instead tell them that you are actively interviewing because hiring managers want what they can’t have. 

#jobinterview #corporate #jobsearch #resume #careeradvice
hook: things I don't want to see in a job interview in under a minute.
transcript: things I don't want to see in a job interview in under a minute. When I greet you, I'm expecting that you shake my hand and I'm expecting that you know how to shake my hand. What is this? Don't do this. Give me a full handshake with eye contact and say it's nice to meet you. I'm going to offer you something to drink. Do not ask for coffee with cream and sugar. I'm not a barista. I'm your interviewer. Just ask for water and say please and thank you. When I walk you into the interview room, do not expect me to show you where you're going to sit. You're not a child. Just sit across from me. When you sit down at the interview table, do not put your hands in your lap or under the table. It makes you look untrustworthy and very nervous. Instead, always put your hands on the table. Throughout the job interview, you are going to be asking me questions and taking notes. Do not take notes on a phone or a laptop. It is too distracting. All you need is a padfolio with a pad of paper. At the end of the job interview, when they say do you have any questions for me, you better have questions prepared and never ever ask me are there any reasons why you don't want to hire me, because, girl, I'm not going to be honest with you. Instead, I want you to tell me that you are actively interviewing, and never come across as desperate because I want what I can't have.

caption:
@barackobama’s best career advice:

1️⃣ “Just know how to get stuff done.”

2️⃣ “Worry more about what you want to do rather than what you want to be.”

Watch @danrothnyc’s full interview with @barackobama via link in bio.
hook: Just learn how to get stuff done. I've seen at every level people who are very good at describing problems, very sophisticated and explaining why something went wrong or why something can't get fixed.
transcript: Just learn how to get stuff done. I've seen at every level people who are very good at describing problems, very sophisticated and explaining why something went wrong or why something can't get fixed. But what I'm always looking for is, no matter how small the problem or how big it is, somebody who says, "Let me take care of that." And if you project an attitude of whatever it is that's needed, I can handle it and I can do it. Whoever is running that organization will notice, I promise. Which is why I think with young people you don't always need to be so impatient asking for the plum assignment. A lot of times the best way to get attention is whatever is assigned to you, you are just nailing. You're killing it. People will notice, oh, that's somebody who can get something done. And the second piece of advice, worry more about what you want to do rather than what you want to be. I think so often people have in their mind I want to be congressman by 30. I want to make x amount of money by this age. The people I find that are most successful are the people who say, man, I'm really interested in computers and figuring this stuff out. And then they end up being a Bill Gates. Or I'm really interested in how to cure this disease. Maybe they don't end up winning the Nobel prize, but you know what? They have an extraordinary career because they're just interested in the thing itself. If you are absorbed by what you're doing, you're going to get really good at it.

caption:
Career advice I needed at 21 instead of 26. 

First ask yourself which person you rather be in the end 

🅰️ “I’m glad I tried it.”
🅱️ “I wish I started sooner.”

Grief changed my perspective on everything. 
I still remember having my laptop out WORKING while my dad laid there sleeping, and sick. 
So this is what I wish I heard earlier. ⬇️

1. Work will always be there. The people you love won’t. 
2. Studying communications means nothing if you never put it into practice. Learn how to communicate and talk to people. 
3. Say “STOP” out loud to your intrusive thoughts when fear comes from a potential thought/project/goal. 
4. Following point #3, write that goal/idea/project down and find label step 1,2, and 3 as an action plan. 
5. If you’re too scared to fail, you don’t deserve to succeed. 
6. Pray about it. I trust God has gone before me to establish my life. Read Proverbs 16. 

TLDR: be bold, take action, shut out the demons whispering you can’t. 
💛 Seek wisdom, good council and family/friends who love and support you.

caption:
In business, leadership, and real growth, the moment you think you’ve arrived is the moment you fall behind.

The loudest person in the room isn’t always the smartest.

The one quoting big names doesn’t always apply what they preach.

And the people who “already know” are usually the ones stuck in their own patterns, unwilling to evolve.

Real leaders are students first.

They don’t fake humility, they live it.

They study the game.

They ask questions even when they have answers.

They don’t perform intelligence, they pursue mastery.

And in a world obsessed with being seen as the expert, being coachable is a power move.

Staying curious is the advantage.

Humility isn’t a weakness, it’s a competitive edge.

This isn’t about being the smartest in the room. It’s about being sharp enough to realize there’s always another level.

The fastest way to fall off is to believe you’ve learned enough.

The winners aren’t the ones with the most opinions. They’re the ones with the most awareness.

Stay focused. Stay teachable. Stay improving while the others stagnate.

So ask yourself:

→Are you building your legacy… or just protecting your ego?

#coralsantoro
hook: You can't teach someone who thinks they already know everything.
transcript: You can't teach someone who thinks they already know everything. You can't help someone who's too proud to ask. And you can't elevate someone who's already placed themselves at the top. The moment you believe you've got nothing left to learn, you stop growing, you stop evolving, you stop winning because real leaders, they're obsessed with learning, they're obsessed with improving. They ask questions, they take notes, they show up like students no matter how successful they are. But the ones who pretend that they know it all, they're not ahead. They're stuck. They're confusing ego with wisdom and applause with results. So here's the truth: the sharpest minds are the most open, the smartest people are the most curious, and the most dangerous person in the room isn't the loud one. It's the one still learning. So stay hungry, stay humble, and let the ones who know it all watch you pass them quietly.

caption:
🚨 Handling being called “the moaner”👇

When you are genuinely concerned about something and need support of management it’s a horrible feeling when they turn around and accuse you of moaning. 

Sometimes this can be a way to avoid dealing with the actual issue and sometimes it can be because of the approach we’re taking. This video is for the latter. 

When you’re raising a concern about an individual’s behaviour I would recommend focusing more on the impact the behaviour is having rather than the behaviour itself using these 4 steps:

1️⃣ Ask for the manager’s advice this is a good way to keep their defences down 

2️⃣ Highlight why you’re concerned and therefore why you’re having the conversation 

3️⃣ Share your concern factually and focus on the impact for example: 

“There have been several occasions recently where [INSERT FACTS], this resulted in XYZ”

4️⃣ Ask them to help influence the situation for example: 

“I really want us to avoid this ever happening again and I need your help influencing [INSERT]”

📌 Please remember the advice offered in this video is generalised and will not fit every situation. Therefore please use your own judgement when using this advice and adapt it to suit your situation. You’ve got this 💪

caption:
What to do when a new hire is underperforming👇

It can be very stressful as a manager when you hire someone and they aren’t performing to the level required. 

In a situation like this open lines of communication are key. Part of your role as a manager is to increase your direct report’s awareness and help them develop so they can perform to the required level. 

It’s important you have realistic expectations. At trap we can all easily fall into is expecting people to arrive as the finished product. 

If they aren’t performing to the level you expect you must make them aware in a supportive and respectful way asap so they have the opportunity to improve. 

Try to avoid criticising them as this is unlikely to get the desired outcome. Instead lead with curiosity and raise their awareness by doing the following:

1️⃣ Ask them how they think things are going. This will give you an idea of their insight and can help you get to know them more. 

2️⃣ Create a safe space. For example: 

“I’m really pleased that you’ve joined the team particularly because of your experience with XYZ so I really want to support you to find your feet so you can contribute your experience fully”

3️⃣ Share what you’ve noticed factually for example missing deadlines.

4️⃣ Ask them what you can do to support them and if they’re not sure spend time exploring this.

📌 Please remember the advice offered in this video is generalised and will not fit every situation. Therefore, please use your own judgement when using this advice and adapt it to suit your situation.

caption:
Five levels of running a 1:1.

Most managers never get past level 2.

Level one.

You show up with no agenda.

You ask "how's everything going?"

They say "yeah good."

You both leave having achieved absolutely nothing.

Level two.

You have an agenda.

Status updates. Project progress. Any blockers.

It's organised. It's also completely forgettable.

You're managing tasks, not a person.

Level three.

You start the meeting with one question.

"What's the most important thing we should talk about today?"

Now they're driving. Now it's their meeting, not yours.

Engagement goes up. Trust goes up. And you start hearing the things people don't usually say to their manager.

Level four.

You come prepared with something for them.

A piece of feedback. An opportunity you spotted. Something you heard in a senior meeting that affects their work.

You're not just receiving. You're bringing something.

That's when people leave a 1:1 feeling like their manager actually invests in them.

Level five.

This is where most managers never get.

You open with this.

"Before we get into the work, how are you actually doing?"

Then you listen. Really listen. No fixing. No advice. Just listening.

Then you say this.

"I want you to know that what you're working on right now is being noticed at the right level. Here's specifically what I've heard."

Then you close with this.

"What's one thing I could do differently that would make your working life easier?"

That last question is the one that changes everything.

Because nobody asks it.

And the manager who does becomes the one their team would run through a wall for.

Tasks get managed at level two.

Careers get built at level five.

Comment RESULTS and find out immediately how to get promoted without playing politics, get that new job and be seen as a leader + get my free audio book

Here are the 5 capabilities ACTUAL leaders need that have nothing to do with being good at their current job:

Leaders see patterns, not just problems. They understand how decisions in one area impact outcomes everywhere else. They think in systems, not silos.

Reading people. Navigating politics. Managing conflict. Building trust. Giving feedback that lands. Having conversations that matter.

Healthcare is in constant flux. Regulations change. Technology evolves. Reimbursements shift. Patient expectations transform.

caption:
Levels of Management: Understanding the Hierarchy in Organizations

In business management, organizations are typically structured into three main levels of management, each responsible for different tasks and decision-making processes:

Top Management – This is the highest level of management, responsible for setting the overall goals, vision, and strategy of the organization. It includes positions like CEO, President, and Board of Directors. They make long-term decisions that impact the entire organization.

Middle Management – Managers at this level interpret and implement the policies and strategies set by top management. They oversee departments or units and ensure that the organization’s objectives are met. Common titles include departmental heads, branch managers, and division managers.

Lower Management – Also known as operational or supervisory management, this level focuses on the day-to-day management of employees and ensuring that tasks are completed efficiently. Supervisors, team leaders, and foremen fall under this category. They directly supervise and guide the workforce.
Each level plays a crucial role in the organizational structure, ensuring that strategic goals are translated into operational actions and that the business runs smoothly at all levels.

If the goal is to make extra income, REITs could help, but know this.

Not all REITs are created the same, even when they both pay investors every single month. Let’s take ORC and EPR. The are two real estate investments, but operate two different ways.

EPR is an experiential REIT that invests in properties tied to experiences like entertainment, attractions, and recreation. ORC is a mortgage REIT, which means instead of primarily owning physical properties, it invests in mortgage-backed securities.

Understand what the company invests in, how it makes money, its dividend history, and the risks involved. The goal is, of course, to collect dividends, but it’s also to understand what you own while building your passive-income strategy.

caption:
Invest in real estate sooner. 

Home equity isn’t just a number on paper—it’s one of the most powerful wealth-building tools available to homeowners. Yet, so many people don’t maximize it.

1️⃣ Pay Down Your Principal Faster – Making just one extra mortgage payment per year or switching to biweekly payments can shave years off your loan and build equity at an accelerated pace.

2️⃣ Invest in Smart Renovations – Not all home improvements boost value. Focus on kitchen remodels, bathroom upgrades, energy-efficient improvements, and curb appeal enhancements—these offer the highest return on investment.

3️⃣ Leverage Market Appreciation – In strong markets (like LA), home values naturally rise over time. Holding onto your property in a growing area can passively increase your equity.

4️⃣ Refinance Strategically – If interest rates drop or your financial situation improves, refinancing into a shorter loan term (like 15 years) can help you build equity significantly faster while saving thousands in interest.

5️⃣ Be Cautious with HELOCs & Cash-Out Refinancing – A Home Equity Line of Credit (HELOC) or cash-out refi can be useful for reinvesting, but overleveraging can put you at risk if market conditions shift. Treat your equity as an asset, not a checking account.

Why does this matter? Because real estate isn’t just about where you live—it’s about long-term financial growth. Managing your equity wisely gives you options: whether it’s upgrading your home, investing in more properties, or securing a stronger financial future.

caption:
If you’re a Real Estate Agent building your own brand, the question isn’t 

❌ “Can I trademark it?”
The real question is: 

✅What do you need to know before you try?

Because I’ve seen way too many real estate professionals spend $$$ on branding — only to find out later that their name isn’t eligible for legal protection.

Let’s break it down:

Tip #1: Think twice before using the word “Realtor” in your official business name.

The word “Realtor” is a federally registered trademark owned by the National Association of Realtors (NAR). All Realtors are real estate agents, but not all real estate agents are Realtors. 
 
Even if you’re a licensed member, you cannot use it freely as part of your brand, business name, or logo. Doing so can get you flagged, fined, or even sued.

NAR has specific guidelines on how the “REALTOR®” trademark can be used, including in marketing materials, on merchandise, and online.

Tip #2: Brand yourself, not your broker.

If your entire online identity is tied to your brokerage… what happens if you leave?
Build a personal brand that lives beyond your current office address — one that clients can follow, remember, and trust wherever your license takes you.

It’s not just smart marketing. It’s long-term freedom.

Tip #3: Consider filing a state trademark if you only operate in one state.

If you’re not ready to serve clients in multiple states and only licensed in (and servicing) one state, a state-level trademark can still give you powerful legal rights — and it’s faster, cheaper, and still gets the job done for local dominance.
